# How to Develop Leadership Skills for Long-Term Success


Published: 11/12/2026


Being good at your job can earn you a leadership role, but it doesn’t automatically prepare you to lead others. The skills that made someone a strong individual contributor don’t always translate to managing people, guiding decisions, or helping a team succeed.


Employees notice the difference. FranklinCovey research finds that[62% of employees](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-great-leader-insight-report?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) say their leader’s management style is outdated, suggesting many leaders haven’t adapted their approach to what teams need today.


The good news is that leadership isn’t a skill you’re simply born with. Rather, it’s something you can develop through practice, feedback, and intentional effort. By focusing on the right skills, leaders can become more effective in their current roles and better prepared for the challenges ahead.


### Key Takeaways:


- Leadership skills can be strengthened through practice, experience, and feedback.
- Most leadership development happens through real-world experience and relationships.
- Strong leadership development combines individual effort with structured support and coaching.


## Leadership Is a Skill Set Built Over Time


## Management is efficiency in climbing the ladder of success; leadership determines whether the ladder is leaning against the right wall.


— Stephen R. Covey


Many people still assume strong leaders are born with a natural gift for it. In truth, experience and reflection develop most of the capabilities that separate effective leaders. That development takes time, even for those who aren’t new to management roles.


Further, management is not the same thing as leadership. While management often refers to titles, leadership is about daily actions and behaviors. And although leadership and management skills may overlap, they draw on different strengths.[Management skills](https://www.franklincovey.com/blog/management-skills/) focus on planning work and keeping it on track, while leadership skills focus on setting direction and helping people commit to it. New leaders often need to make several deliberate mindset shifts to move from one to the other.


Leadership skills shape how a person guides a team toward shared goals. They influence how leaders communicate, make decisions, build trust, and help others grow. These skills determine not just how well a leader performs, but how well their entire team succeeds.


## The Core Leadership Skills Worth Developing


Effective leaders share a core set of[capabilities](https://www.franklincovey.com/blog/leadership-competencies/) that help them guide teams and get results. Five of them form a strong foundation for leadership development:


- **Communication –** Clear expectations supported by the discipline to listen well.
- **Adaptability –** The judgment to adjust a leadership approach to the person and the situation.
- **Strategic thinking –** The capacity to make sound decisions with incomplete information.
- **Trust-building –** Consistent behavior that gives people confidence in a leader’s character.
- **Coaching –** A focus on developing others rather than solving every problem personally.

## How to Develop Leadership Skills Through Deliberate Practice


Knowing which skills matter is only the starting point. The following six practices help leaders turn that knowledge into consistent behavior their teams can see.


### 1. Identify Strengths and Blind Spots


Leadership development begins with an accurate picture of where a leader stands today, and most leaders overestimate their own clarity. Research suggests that[95% of people](https://www.forbes.com/sites/jeffkauflin/2017/05/10/only-15-of-people-are-self-aware-heres-how-to-change/) believe they are self-aware, while only 10% to 15% actually are. Leaders can close this gap through a few consistent practices, outlined below.


- **360-degree assessments:** Structured input from peers and direct reports that reveals patterns a leader may not notice alone.
- **Candid conversations:** Regular check-ins with trusted colleagues about how specific interactions landed or how leaders are being perceived.
- **Personal reflection:** A brief review after key meetings or decisions that compares what a leader intended with how others responded.


The goal is to understand how others see their leadership, since a leader’s actions affect a team more than their intentions do.


### 2. Stay Composed Under Pressure


## Leadership is a choice that lies in the space between stimulus and response.


— Stephen R. Covey


A leader’s response under pressure directly impacts trust with their teams, as it affects how comfortable people feel raising important concerns. Leaders should handle situations intentionally rather than reacting automatically. Taking a moment to pause before responding gives them more control and helps them act in ways that reflect their values.


A leader’s composure also sets the standard for everyone else. People tend to mirror how their leader handles pressure, so a steady response to a tight deadline or a missed target encourages the same behavior across the team.


### 3. Listen Before Responding


Listening is a critical[communication](https://www.franklincovey.com/blog/leadership-communication-skills/) skill that often stays underdeveloped. Many leaders listen with the intent to reply rather than to understand others, which leads them to miss the concern behind the question.


Leaders who[seek first to understand](https://www.franklincovey.com/habit-5/) ask clarifying questions and reflect back what they heard before offering a view of their own. This habit also helps improve difficult conversations, since people who feel heard are less likely to become defensive.


### 4. Pursue Leadership Coaching


[Executive coaching](https://www.franklincovey.com/coaching/executive-coaching/) helps senior leaders inspire others and drive results with greater clarity and purpose. The most effective coaching is time-bound and measured against mutually set objectives, which helps leaders translate coaching into meaningful and lasting results. Throughout the coaching experience, executives work together with a coach to identify challenges, build practical leadership skills, strengthen decision-making, and prepare for future responsibilities.


Executive coaching can support leaders through different stages and challenges in their careers:


- **Developmental coaching** helps leaders thrive in their current role or prepare for what’s next by identifying their natural style and adapting their approach to meet the evolving needs of their team and organization.
- **Transition coaching** accelerates success for newly promoted or external executives by shortening the onboarding curve.
- **Agility coaching** strengthens adaptability, focus, and resilience so leaders can lead through rapid change with a growth-oriented mindset.


Coaching can come from an external party, a mentor, or a more experienced leader within the organization. An[executive coach](https://www.franklincovey.com/blog/what-is-executive-coaching/) gives a leader an objective outside perspective on habits that are hard to see from the inside. Through structured conversations, a coach can help a leader to spot patterns in how they make decisions, run meetings, or handle conflict.

### 5. Seek Regular Feedback


Leaders who ask for feedback regularly, rather than waiting for an annual review, can correct course while the stakes are still small. Asking specific questions usually leads to more useful feedback. For example, a leader who asks, “What is one thing I could do to make our team meetings more productive?” is more likely to get a candid, actionable response than a leader who asks, “How am I doing?”


The way a leader responds to feedback matters as much as the request itself. Thanking people for[honest input](https://www.franklincovey.com/courses/6-critical-practices/use-feedback-as-fuel/) and acting on it shows that speaking up is valued and encourages people to share feedback again.


The same principle applies to the feedback leaders give. Gallup data shows that employees who receive feedback weekly or more often are[far more likely to be engaged (48%)](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/651812/organizations-redefine-feedback-including-recognition.aspx) than those who receive it annually or less (5%). Leaders who consistently seek and offer feedback build a team culture where people treat it as a normal part of improvement.


### 6. Prioritize Self-Renewal


Leaders often put their own growth and well-being last because team and business needs come first. Over time, this can weaken the skills and abilities they need to lead well. Additionally, leadership skills fade without regular maintenance, and growing responsibilities often call for new capabilities. Leaders who embrace the principle of[Habit 7: Sharpen the Saw](https://www.franklincovey.com/courses/the-7-habits/habit-7/) ™ set aside regular time to renew their skills, knowledge, and energy.


Self-renewal works best when it covers several areas of a leader’s life:


- **Body.** Exercising, eating well, and getting enough sleep to sustain energy and manage stress.
- **Heart.** Investing in key relationships through consistent deposits of time and trust.
- **Mind.** Growing knowledge and skill through reading, writing, learning, and creating.
- **Spirit.** Spending time on activities that align with a leader’s deepest values, such as performing service for others, reflection, or time in nature.


Leaders can make renewal practical by scheduling it and treating it as a non-negotiable responsibility. Blocking time on the calendar for learning, exercise, or reflection treats development as a commitment instead of an afterthought. Leaders who renew themselves consistently keep their skills current as responsibilities grow. They also show their teams that development never finishes, and that these self-renewal activities are essential for long-term fulfillment.

## Great Leaders Develop the Leaders Around Them


## Telling reinforces dependency; coaching develops capability.


— Paul Walker, CEO, FranklinCovey


Organizations that want to learn[how to develop leadership skills](https://www.franklincovey.com/blog/developing-leaders-in-your-organization/) in the workplace often find that the most effective development happens between leaders and the people they manage. A leader who invests in the growth of others extends their impact well beyond their own role.


FranklinCovey research shows that[only 7% of leaders](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-great-leader-insight-report?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) combine high expectations for performance with high support for their people. Leaders who[coach potential](https://www.franklincovey.com/courses/4essentialroles/role-4-coach-potential/) in others recognize their strengths and give them opportunities that match their readiness. Showing confidence in their ability to grow can also help emerging leaders feel more confident taking on new challenges.


A structured[leadership development plan](https://www.franklincovey.com/blog/leadership-development-plan/) keeps coaching consistent. Leaders and team members can agree on which skills to focus on and find opportunities to practice them through their regular work. Leaders who develop others this way prepare more people to take on leadership roles and reduce organizational reliance on any one person.


## Stronger Leadership Skills Create Stronger Organizational Results


Strong leadership capability compounds over time, shaping how teams perform, how long people stay, and how well organizations adapt. FranklinCovey analysis reveals that high-trust organizations experience[50% lower turnover](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-ai-transformation-human-imperative?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) than low-trust organizations, along with 41% lower absenteeism. Leaders who build trust through consistent actions help create an environment where people want to stay and do their best work.
